Text is not the only source of vectors. Later chapters on visual, audio, and video features describe images, sounds, and video shots by vectors of low-level perceptual features, such as the distribution of colors in an image. These features differ from embeddings in how they are obtained: a hand-designed extraction rule computes them directly from the signal. They also differ in how they are compared. Perceptual features usually come with a distance, such as Euclidean distance, where a smaller value means a better match. As with embeddings, the comparison function belongs to the feature. It follows from how the feature was defined or learned, and we cannot simply replace it with another one.

For both approaches, the search task is the same. A linear scan compares the query with every stored vector and returns the best matches. A better approach organizes the vectors in advance, as the inverted file does for sparse vectors, so that a query visits only a small part of the collection. This task is the

. It is well understood in two and three dimensions, where geographic information systems and computer graphics have solved it for decades. With embeddings of hundreds or thousands of dimensions, it has gained new interest. This section formalizes what a best match is, first under a similarity score and then under a distance. The rest of the chapter asks how to find the best matches without a full scan.

Normalizing the query does no harm, and it is useful when scores must be comparable across queries, for example against a fixed similarity threshold. For ranking alone, it is not required.
To see how a perceptual feature turns media into a vector, consider the color content of an image.

splits a photograph into its red, green, and blue channels and summarizes each channel by a histogram over its 256 intensity values. To build the histograms, we visit every pixel and increase three bins by one: the bin for the pixel’s red intensity in the red histogram, and likewise for green and blue. The three histograms together hold

children.html: 3×256=7683 \times 256 = 7683×256=768

children.value: counts, which we read as a 768-dimensional feature vector of the image.

children.alt: A color image split into its red, green, and blue channels, each summarized by an intensity histogram.

children.value: A color image split into its red, green, and blue channels, each summarized by an intensity histogram.

Exact intensities are too fine-grained for comparing images. Two photographs of the same pasta under slightly different light would share hardly any bins. We therefore quantize each histogram into fewer, wider bins, for example 16 bins per channel that each cover 16 intensity values. Similar shades now fall into the same bin, and the feature vector shrinks to

children.html: 3×16=483 \times 16 = 483×16=48

children.value: values, each counting the pixels in one bin.

To compare two images by their colors, we sum the absolute differences of their counts over all 48 bins. Two images with similar color distributions differ little in every bin and receive a small sum. A photograph of a blue sky differs strongly from the red pasta in many bins and receives a large sum. This sum is the Manhattan distance between the two feature vectors. The color histogram is deliberately simple: it only shows how image content is reduced to a vector. Later chapters introduce more expressive perceptual features.

children.value: reverses the direction of comparison: a smaller value means a better match, and identical vectors have distance zero. Most distances used in retrieval are metrics, which means they are non-negative, symmetric, and satisfy the triangle inequality. Each distance induces a different notion of a neighborhood, that is, a different shape for the set of points within a fixed distance of a center.
(L2) measures straight-line distance and gives a round neighborhood. It is the default for continuous features.
(L1) sums the absolute differences per dimension and gives a diamond neighborhood. It emphasizes many small differences.
(L-infinity) takes the single largest component difference and gives a square neighborhood. It lets the worst dimension dominate.
weights and correlates the dimensions through a matrix, giving a tilted-ellipse neighborhood.

children.alt: Neighborhood shapes of four distance measures in 2D: Euclidean (round), Manhattan (diamond), maximum (square), and quadratic (tilted ellipse).

Embeddings rarely need further adjustment, because every dimension comes from the same learned space and lives on a comparable scale. Perceptual features are different. A feature vector often combines values that were measured independently, and the color histogram shows two forms of the resulting problem.

Whether we maximize a similarity score or minimize a distance, we now have a precise definition of the best matches. The rest of the chapter answers a single question about these definitions: how do we compute the arg-max or arg-min without comparing the query to every stored vector? For a few thousand vectors a full scan is fine. For millions or billions it is not, and the structures that speed up the search behave very differently depending on how many dimensions the vectors have.

Compute dot product, cosine, and Euclidean and Manhattan distances on the same vectors, watch length normalization make cosine and dot product agree, and see Gaussian normalization rebalance dimensions on different scales.
